Dongyu “Don” Han / Research engineer

A network is vast.
Our view is small.

A rapid valve closure launches a transient pressure wave through the pipes. We record the resulting pressure response at only a handful of sensors. My research asks what those signals can reveal about a leak—and where we should measure them.

The challenge

The network is mapped.
The leak is not.

A leak can change how transient pressure waves reflect and scatter through the pipes. But labeled field measurements are scarce, and every additional sensor costs money and effort. That leads to two connected questions: how can a model learn from limited measured responses, and where should we place the sensors?

01 Learn across the gap

Start in simulation.
Test in the field.

We can simulate many leak scenarios, but collect only a small number of labeled transient pressure responses in the field. Simulations give a model a starting point; measured responses let us test and adapt it to the physical network.

I fine-tuned models trained on simulated transients using limited experimental measurements. I then used Integrated Gradients to inspect which sensor–time regions contributed most to their predictions.

Transfer learning · Interpretable leak diagnosis
THE QUESTION

Can features learned from simulated transients still help when the model meets measured responses?

What changed

On the original experimental dataset, fine-tuning substantially reduced the best model’s leak-location error.

Best leak-location MAE

Transformer model · 17 experimental scenarios

13.51 m Direct simulation-to-field test→1.02 m After field-data fine-tuning

Mean absolute error on this evaluation; lower is better. These are best-model results, not a general field-performance guarantee.

02 Choose where to measure

When you cannot
measure everywhere.

Even a strong model is limited by what its sensors record. In a larger network, adding sensors at every node is impractical; each location has to earn its place.

I built a method that learns which subset of locations is most useful for distinguishing leak events. The network below shows the branches and nodes; the changing selection probabilities show the model making that choice during training.

Contrastive learning · Sensor selection
What changed

Choosing sensors for the task—not just spreading them across the pipes—can improve what the model recognizes.

Classification accuracy

One simulated Q‑Leak setting · 8 sensors · SNR = 0 dB

%
Information-based selection (MI/MaxDet)
73.93
Task-aligned selection (DCSS)
86.62

At some lower-SNR, tighter-budget settings, the MI/MaxDet baseline performs better. This comparison uses simulated responses, not field measurements.
